Fair challenge. Honest answer: no. What I wrote is a faithful execution of the handover's prescribed split, and it is a real improvement, but three things in it are the handover's shape rather than my best judgement.

**Where I was constrained, and what I'd do instead**

1. *Stateful collaborators instead of immutable snapshots.* I gave you `AptFileState`, `Keyrings`, `Collateral` — objects holding the same 35 mutable fields, just partitioned. The better cut is by *phase*, not by subsystem: one per-machine reader producing a frozen `/etc/apt` + package snapshot; a pure `AptPlanner(source_snapshot, target_snapshot, decision_files) -> AptPlan`; a pure `accept_review(plan, outcome) -> AptChangeSet` (derived writes in order, keyring writes, approved group diffs, approved collateral, package→dest attribution, origin holds); an applier that drives the change set. Then `_origin_refusals: dict | None`, `_repo_group_outcome: dict | None` and `_metadata_refreshed` stop existing — all three are lazy-memoisation sentinels that only exist because one long-lived object is re-entered from the base loop. I expect that also drops most of the executor faking in the 6792-line test file, since the planning half becomes pure functions.

2. *The transactional `/etc/apt` group is smuggled through the base loop.* `PackageSyncJob.apply()` calls `converge()` per diff, so the group fakes atomicity: the first group diff does all the work, the rest read a cached outcome map, and a synthetic `apt:metadata-refresh` diff exists to give the group somewhere to hang. That produces `_record_group_failure`, the documented `KeyError` hazard (apt_sync.py:3307-3315), and the outcome latch. The fix is a `converge_group` seam in `packages/sync_core.py`. I did not propose it because it touches code shared with three other jobs and it changes observable output (the marker's per-item apply log line and its dry-run preview line disappear) — the handover forbids behaviour change in Step 1. It belongs in an ADR, not smuggled into a restructure.

3. *Padding to a line floor.* I put `/etc/apt` path constants in `items.py` and `MetadataRefresh` in `commands.py` to avoid ~60-line modules, because the handover says "150–600 lines each". A shared vocabulary module is exactly where a small file is right. Under (1), `MetadataRefresh` doesn't exist at all.

One thing I'd keep regardless: `files.py` (staging → `sudo install` → backup) is a genuine seam, and I'd widen it to own *every* target file mutation so `repo_group.py` holds no shell strings.

1 # Package sync — user requirements 2 3 What package synchronisation does, what it asks the user, and what it will not do. 4 5 ## Navigation 6 7 - [High level requirements](high-level-requirements.md) — project vision and scope 8 - [Package sync conformance criteria](package-sync-conformance-criteria.md) — these requirements as individually checkable obligations 9 - [Package sync job behaviour](../jobs/package-sync.md) — user guide 10 - [ADR-020](../adr/adr-020-declarative-package-convergence.md) — the decision record and the reasoning behind it 11 12 This document states the intent. Where it and any other document disagree, this one is right. 13 14 ## What package sync is for 15 16 Work on one machine, sync, resume on the other. That only works if the software is there: a synced home directory on a machine without the applications gives configuration for programs that will not start. 17 18 Package sync replicates *what software is installed*. Application data belongs to folder sync, which must run after it — installing software writes its own stock defaults, and those have to land before the user's synced settings go on top of them. 19 20 It replicates by **convergence, not by copying**. Both machines' package managers are asked what they have, and the difference is what the sync acts on; no package database, store or installed file is copied between machines. What is synced is a decision — install this, remove that — plus the configuration the target's own package manager needs to carry it out. 21 22 Package sync is one job per package manager — apt, snap, flatpak — plus a job for software no package manager can reproduce. Each is enabled separately, reviewed separately, and can fail without stopping the others. Enabling one authorises pc-switcher to install and remove software on the target. 23 24 ## Vocabulary 25 26 **Source** and **target** are per-run roles. The sync is launched on the source; the target is the machine being changed. The next run may swap them. 27 28 **The holding machine** is the machine that has the item being decided about — the source for something it has and the target lacks, the target for something only the target has. 29 30 An **item** is one thing the user can be asked about: a package, a snap, a flatpak application, an apt hold, a flatpak mask, a configuration file. Its identity is stable across runs, so a decision about it can be remembered. 31 32 A **decision** is the user's answer about an item: apply it, skip it this run, or always skip it in future runs. 33 34 **Machine-specific** describes an item marked "always skip". The job that marked it never touches that item again on that machine of its own accord, whichever machine the sync runs from — it is neither sent to the other machine nor changed by it. Where an approved change would touch it anyway, the user is asked first. 35 36 **Derived** describes plumbing that is synced because approved software needs it — the repository a package comes from, its signing key, a pin, a flatpak remote. It is never a question of its own. 37 38 An **origin** is where software actually comes from — a repository or remote URL. Not its name: two remotes can share a name and serve different builds. 39 40 A **snippet** is a shell recipe, written once, for software no package manager can install. 41 42 **Flatpak scope** is the user or system flatpak installation. **Snap revision** and **snap channel** are the exact build and the update track. 43 44 ## The model 45 46 **A sync goes one way, from source to target.** The source's installed state is what will be replicated on the target. 47 48 **Identity includes the origin.** `gh` from GitHub's repository and `gh` from Ubuntu's archive share a name and are different software. A package is installed on the target from the same origin it has on the source. 49 50 **The user is asked about software; the plumbing is derived.** Approving a package also approves the repository it comes from — a repository without its package does nothing, and a package without its repository cannot be installed. 51 52 **Consent precedes every change.** Nothing is written to the target before the user has approved the changes that job proposes. 53 54 Where an answer follows from something already approved, it is not asked again. Where it does not, it is asked. 55 56 Asking about every package separately would interrupt the user constantly, so questions are gathered into reviews, and repeated decisions of one kind are presented as a single list settled in one pass. That is a preference, not a rule: applying an approved change can reveal something the plan could not know, and a further question is then correct. 57 58 Approving a removal takes a gesture distinct from approving an install, and is never the default. 59 60 **A failure lands on the package it concerns**, or on the configuration item itself where no package is involved. Every approved item is attempted and every failure is named. If a pin, repository or key fails to land, the packages that needed it fail with it, rather than being installed from whatever origin the machine would otherwise use. 61 62 ```mermaid 63 flowchart TD 64 A["plan — reads only"] --> B["review — the user decides"] 65 B --> C["apply the approved changes"] 66 C --> D["report, per item"] 67 C -.->|"an applied change reveals
something the plan could not know"| E["a further question"] 68 E -.-> C 69 ``` 70 71 ## What happens during a sync 72 73 In its validation step, pc-switcher checks every enabled job's prerequisites before any of them changes anything — core behaviour, not specific to package sync. apt additionally refuses to start while the target's dpkg lock is held. 74 75 Snap auto-refresh is paused on both machines for the run and restored afterwards. The pause is timed, so it expires by itself if the run dies. 76 77 Each job then plans, reviews, applies and reports. 78 79 **Plan** issues read commands only: what each machine has, filtered by the standing machine-specific marks, and the difference between them. A question that cannot be derived is asked here rather than in the review — [apt's Ubuntu Pro question (see below)](#esm-repositories--ubuntu-pro) is one, because one of its answers ends the job before there is anything to review. 80 81 **Review** presents one group at a time: items of one kind, all doing the same thing, each carrying its own decision and all settled in a single pass. The default choice for each item is the action that does no harm: *apply* for an install, *skip* for anything that removes or overwrites. Three answers are offered, or two where a permanent decision is not meaningful. 82 83 The two machines are named by hostname wherever the user reads them, and every answer states its effect on a named machine — the skip answer on a removal reads *keep it on MyMachine*, not "skip". The user can abort the whole sync at any question, and aborting is never read as declining one item. 84 85 **Apply** converges one item at a time, in the order the job requires, and announces every write. Nothing unapproved is written, and no write escapes pc-switcher's per-command confirmation — including the decision records, the snippet registry and the snap refresh pause. 86 87 **Report** gives the job's outcome: success, skipped with the reason, or failed naming each failed item. 88 89 The log holds more than the report. It names every item the job presented and the decision each one got, and every change the package manager made on its own behalf — the collateral the review never showed. The package manager's own output is kept verbatim in the debug log. 90 91 A credential embedded in a URL is withheld wherever the user or the log would otherwise see it — in a command, in a package manager's output, in a configuration file shown whole for a decision. A repository can carry its password in its own address, and a log file is readable by anyone with an account on the machine that wrote it. 92 93 A **dry run** plans and reviews exactly as a real run does — the questions are still asked — then changes nothing and records nothing. A **non-interactive run** — one with no terminal to answer at, such as from cron or a script — asks nothing, treats every item as declined, and reports any job with a non-empty review as skipped. 94 95 ## Decisions and their memory: "machine specific" 96 97 **Apply** does the thing. **Skip** declines it for this run only. **Always skip** marks the item as **machine-specific**. The mark is recorded on the **holding machine** — not necessarily the machine the sync was launched from. 98 99 Example: two machines Atlas and Vega, sync launched from Atlas. Vega has `steam`; Atlas does not, so the sync offers to remove it from Vega. Answering "always skip" writes the mark **on Vega**, because Vega holds `steam`. The reverse case: Atlas has `wireshark`, the sync offers to install it on Vega, and "always skip" writes the mark on **Atlas**. 100 101 A machine-specific item is filtered out before the difference is computed, so it never appears in a later review. Because of that, the repository-conflict question below has to disclose it explicitly. 102 103 Marks never sync between machines. Snippets do, because how to install something is knowledge about the software rather than the machine. 104 105 Repositories and pins cannot be marked machine-specific, whether they are being added, changed or deleted; a flatpak remote is never asked about at all, so there is nothing to mark. Where the two machines disagree about where software comes from, that disagreement keeps surfacing every run instead of being silenced once, and the remedy is to align the two machines. apt's own configuration files *can* be marked, because they say how apt behaves rather than where software comes from. 106 107 Report-only findings cannot be marked either — no machine holds a version difference, and a mark would stop the package syncing rather than stop the report. 108 109 ## apt 110 111 apt sync covers the **manually installed** package set — what the user asked for, not what apt pulled in to satisfy it. With it are synced the repositories and pins that decide where those packages come from, apt's own configuration, and apt holds. 112 113 ### Installing 114 115 ```mermaid 116 flowchart TD 117 A["On the source,
absent on the target"] --> B{"Where did the
source get it?"} 118 B -->|"the distribution"| C["Ordinary install"] 119 B -->|"elsewhere"| D{"Does the target already
offer it from that origin?"} 120 D -->|yes| C 121 D -->|no| E{"Can the source's origin
be replicated?"} 122 E -->|yes| F["Install, naming the origin.
Its repository, key and pin
are synced as a consequence"] 123 E -->|no| G["Report it, with origin
and reason. Do not install"] 124 F --> H{"After the configuration lands,
what would apt really install?"} 125 H -->|"the source's origin"| I["Install"] 126 H -->|otherwise| J["Refuse this one install,
naming both origins.
Continue the run"] 127 ``` 128 129 The review names the origin whenever an install would come from anything other than the distribution. 130 131 The last step is a real check against the target's own state after the configuration has landed, not a prediction. An install that would come from the wrong origin fails alone, naming both, and the run continues. 132 133 Two machines on different Ubuntu mirrors are not two origins: each machine's own distribution source files define what "the distribution" means for it. 134 135 A package from a hand-downloaded `.deb` is not apt-sync's business — see [*Software no manager can reproduce*](#software-no-manager-can-reproduce). 136 137 ### Removing a package 138 139 A package on the target that the source lacks is offered for removal, with "skip" selected as default action. Removal does not purge the package's configuration. 140 141 ### Reporting without acting 142 143 Same package, same origin, same version shows nothing at all. 144 145 Three situations are reported and never acted on: 146 147 - **different versions** — both named; versions float — package managers handle updates, not pc-switcher 148 - **different origins** — both named; takes precedence over a version difference, and is never reported for a mirror difference 149 - **an origin that cannot be replicated** — warning reported with the reason, never installed from somewhere else 150 151 ### Holds 152 153 An apt hold is its own item, decided separately from its package, both when it is added and when it is removed. 154 155 A hold blocks everything: apt will not install, upgrade or remove a held package, not even as an unused dependency. So it serves two intents at once — "never lose this" and "never move this off the version that works" — and apt gives no way to tell them apart. 156 157 That second intent decides how a held package is installed. Everywhere else a version floats, because the user expressed no preference; a hold *is* that preference. So when the source holds a package the target lacks, the target gets the **source's exact version**, not whatever repositories currently offer. If that version is no longer available on the target, the install fails as its own item naming both versions — better than silently freezing the target on a version the user never chose, which nothing would ever move again. 158 159 ### Collateral damage 160 161 Approving an install can make apt remove or downgrade something else, through *conflicts*, *replaces* or version constraints. 162 163 If apt installed that something automatically, the collateral action proceeds silently — apt is resolving its own dependencies. The log names it. 164 165 If it is **manually installed on the target**, the user is asked first about any removal/downgrade/upgrade. The question names the package, says that this machine's apt has it marked manually installed, and says what the approved change would do to it. Three answers, each stating its effect: install anyway, skip and leave the triggering install unapplied, or stop the whole apt sync. 166 167 A package marked **machine-specific** is the case that matters most, and the question mentions explicitly that the package is machine specific. 168 169 A package the user chose to keep is protected too. Only a removal the user *approved* is exempt from this question, and one skipped for this run, or marked machine-specific, keeps its protection. A decision made earlier in this same run counts. 170 171 Declining cancels only the changes that actually cause the collateral. Where several cause it together, all are cancelled and the question says so. It never overwrites a decision the user already gave. 172 173 ### Repositories, keys and pins 174 175 Adding or changing a repository is never a question: it is written because an approved package comes from it, and one that feeds nothing this run syncs is not synced at all. 176 177 Deleting one is a question, but only once nothing on the target still uses it — counted after this run's approved removals, and counting packages marked machine-specific. While anything still uses it, the repository stays and is never raised. The question names the URLs the file declares, not just its filename. 178 179 A repository both machines have with different content is overwritten with the source's version silently — unless the overwrite would repoint a package the target marked machine-specific. Then the user is asked, and shown both versions of the file in full. Declining fails every approved package whose origin depended on that file. 180 181 Only a repository this run writes because an approved package comes from it can raise that question. A differing file nothing approved this run needs, is not written, so there is nothing to consent to. 182 183 The distribution's own source files are written and updated, never removed or offered for removal. Files apt itself does not read are not treated as repository configuration. 184 185 **Signing keys are never a review item.** A key the target lacks is copied byte-for-byte from the source before the repository naming it is written; one that differs is refreshed, unless the target's own distribution packaging owns it. Keys are synced from the source machine, not fetched from the internet. An approved repository deletion may take an unreferenced key with it. 186 187 **Every** pin the source has is written to the target, always, without review: a pin decides which origin wins, and one naming an absent origin does nothing. Deleting a pin only the target has *is* reviewed, and the file is shown whole. 188 189 A pin is never read as a statement about the packages it names. 190 191 apt's own configuration — proxy settings, recommends policy — is reviewed whether it is being added, changed or removed, with the full decision, because no approved package implies whether such a setting should be synced. 192 193 ### ESM repositories — Ubuntu Pro 194 195 If the source carries ESM repositories and the target reports no Ubuntu Pro attachment, the user is asked before anything is written and before any other apt question. Two answers: attach the target now, or skip apt for this run while everything else proceeds. The user is told what to run on the target to attach it. 196 197 Writing them to an unattached target fails invisibly: `apt-get update` succeeds and the failure surfaces later, as a 401 during some unrelated install. pc-switcher cannot attach the target itself. 198 199 "I have attached it" re-probes rather than taking the answer on trust, and may be answered any number of times. Skipping skips the whole apt job, not just the ESM files, leaving apt's configuration untouched. A non-interactive run takes the skip; a dry run warns instead. 200 201 Only whether the target is attached is ever logged or shown. 202 203 ### Applying apt's changes 204 205 All repository-configuration work is applied as one unit: backed up, written in apt's required order, then one refresh of the package lists. If the refresh fails, everything is restored and every approved package that depended on the unit fails by name. If a restore itself fails, the backup is kept and its path named. 206 207 Every derived change is logged as it lands and appears in a dry run's preview. 208 209 ## snap 210 211 snap follows the shape every job has: what the source has is offered for install, what only the target has for removal, what cannot be converged is reported. What is particular to snap: 212 213 ### Revision and channel 214 215 snap converges the source's **exact revision and channel**, where apt and flatpak let versions float: snap keeps per-user data in `~/snap///`, which folder sync can only mirror correctly when both machines are on the same revision. 216 217 So a difference of revision or channel is a change to apply, naming both values, rather than something reported; an install lands the source's revision and channel on the target; and the same revision and channel on both machines produces nothing. 218 219 ### Removing a snap 220 221 Removing a snap leaves snapd's own pre-removal snapshot in place — the only recovery path if the removal was a mistake. 222 223 ### Refresh holds 224 225 Refresh holds replicate as their own items, both when added and when removed. A hold recorded for a snap the source no longer has produces no item. 226 227 ### Sideloaded snaps 228 229 Snaps installed from a local `.snap` file are out of scope (#221). They are ignored on both machines: never installed, never removed, never an item. A run names the ones it found so the user knows they are unmanaged, and does nothing else about them. 230 231 ## flatpak 232 233 flatpak follows the shape every job has: what the source has is offered for install, what only the target has for removal, what cannot be converged is reported. What is particular to flatpak: 234 235 ### Identity 236 237 A flatpak application is identified by its **scope** and its **full reference including branch**. The same application in both scopes, or on two branches, is two independent items — one install and one removal — reported as found. 238 239 Origin is not part of that identity: flatpak refuses to install a reference already present from a different remote, so a difference of origin is reported rather than converged, and takes precedence over a version difference. 240 241 ### Installing an application 242 243 An application is installed from the source's remote or not at all, and that remote is identified by **URL and verification setting, never by name** — checked before the install and read back after it. Either failure fails that one application. 244 245 ### Remotes 246 247 A remote is never a review item, whether it is being added, changed or deleted. It is plumbing, derived from the applications the user approved. 248 249 There is no distribution remote to start from: a remote is synced only because an approved application needs it — including the remote supplying that application's runtime — and is provisioned before the first install. 250 251 **A remote replicates with its trust**, not just its name and URL: its signing key is synced byte-for-byte from the source, a verified remote is never replicated as unverified, and an unverified one is replicated as such with a warning. 252 253 A remote both machines have whose URL or verification differs is repointed silently — unless that would move the origin of a machine-specific application, in which case the user is asked, shown both configurations, and declining fails every approved application that needed the source's URL. 254 255 One the source does not have is deleted once nothing on the target still uses it — after this run's approved removals, counted against what the machine actually has, including applications marked machine-specific. While anything still uses it, it stays. Deleting a remote takes its signing key with it. 256 257 A remote the source restricts with a filter is replicated **with its filter**. The filter is a separate file at a path of the user's choosing — flatpak records the path, not the content — so it is copied byte-for-byte to the same path on the target and re-applied there. Like a signing key, it is derived and never a review item. It is applied after the approved applications from that remote have landed, because a filter can be narrower than what the source has installed and must not block replicating it. If it cannot land, every approved application from that remote fails. 258 259 ### Masks and scopes 260 261 Mask patterns replicate per scope, added and removed alike, whether or not anything currently matches them, and land after the applications. 262 263 A flatpak installation that is neither the user nor the system one is skipped. 264 265 ## Software no manager can reproduce 266 267 Software that arrived on the source by a route nothing can replay automatically. Several kinds, one mechanism: the **install snippet**, a shell recipe written once that is synced with the software. 268 269 - **A hand-downloaded `.deb`** — apt knows the name, but no configured repository offers that version. 270 - **Unowned software under `/usr/local` or `/opt`** — dropped there by an install script or a tarball. The scan is deliberately shallow: it names a finding so the user can decide, it does not walk a tree. 271 - **A sideloaded snap**, and **a flatpak from a local bundle or a dead remote** — out of scope for now (#221). 272 273 Detection runs on the **source** only, so there is no record of what was installed this way on the target and **nothing here is ever removed**. 274 275 Every detected item ends the run with a snippet, marked machine-specific, or skipped for this run. 276 277 A snippet is **opaque** — stored and replayed exactly as written, never parsed. It runs as the target user with no privilege added around it and no standing input, so a command expecting an answer fails rather than hanging the sync. 278 279 Reproducibility is judged by what the **source** holds. The snippet registry is synced; if that would lose or change an entry only the target has, the user is asked and declining aborts the run. A snippet written during a review is replayed in that same run. 280 281 ## When something goes wrong 282 283 Every approved item is attempted, and all failures are reported together, each naming its item. One failed item does not block the rest of its job; one failed job does not stop the others. 284 285 A repository, key, pin or remote has no item of its own to fail on. When one of them fails to land, that failure is charged to every approved package that needed it, and all of those packages fail — including ones that would otherwise have installed, because the origin they were approved for is not there. 286 287 It does not work the other way round. A package that fails to install leaves the repository it came from in place, and leaves the other packages that share it untouched. 288 289 A read that does not answer is different. If a package manager cannot be queried at all, its silence is never read as "this machine has nothing installed", which would propose removing everything on the other machine. It fails once, naming the command, and it fails only its own job — the other jobs still run. An *empty* answer is ordinary data. 290 291 ## What this deliberately does not do 292 293 - **The target's apt configuration is not under line-by-line control.** Repositories, keys and pins appear because a package was approved; declining the package is the only way to decline them. 294 - **A pin cannot be kept on one machine only.** It is asked about every run until source and target have the same pin. 295 - **Version drift and origin divergence are reported, never resolved**, for apt and flatpak. 296 - **Hand-installed software is never removed from the target.** 297 - **A target with no Ubuntu Pro attachment costs the whole apt job for that run.** 298 - **A non-interactive run can answer no review.** There is no file of standing answers and no assume-yes option. 299 - **Machine-specific marks are per job, per machine, and never synced.** 300

1	# Package sync divergences
2	
3	
4	Two seeds from the planning stage were checked and did **not** hold up: dry run does show and answer the review, which is what `PKG-FR-DRY-RUN` asks for; and `--confirm-each-command` does cover the decision records, the snippet registry and the refresh pause, as `PKG-FR-CONFIRM-EACH` requires. Neither is a divergence.
5	
6	## DIV-01 — A failed probe ends the whole run, contradicting the stated failure isolation
7	
8	`PKG-FR-OUTCOME-FAILED` requires that "one failed job MUST NOT stop the others". The orchestrator honours that for `PackageItemFailures` only: that arm records FAILED and continues (`orchestrator.py:1292-1314`). `ProbeFailed` is a plain `RuntimeError` (`probes.py:37`), so it falls through to `except Exception`, which records FAILED and then re-raises (`orchestrator.py:1315-1335`), ending the run.
9	
10	Whether this is wrong depends on which reading is intended. `probes.py:42-48` argues a probe failure means the machine or the tool is broken, which is not a finding about any item and arguably *should* stop everything. `PKG-FR-OUTCOME-FAILED` does not distinguish the two. **Ruling needed:** does a dead package-manager read fail its own job and let the others run, or stop the sync?
11	
12	## DIV-02 — The automation escape hatch writes permanent state and is documented nowhere
13	
14	`PCSWITCHER_PACKAGE_REVIEW_AUTOMATION` takes a JSON `item_id → decision` map and bypasses every prompt, returning `was_interactive=True` (`review.py:580-582`). Because the permanence guards test exactly that flag (`sync_core.py:454`, `manual_installs_sync.py:583`), this path **writes machine-specific marks and install snippets** — the two things `PKG-FR-SKIP-ONCE` and `PKG-FR-MACHINE-SPECIFIC` describe as coming from an explicit human choice.
15	
16	It is deliberately absent from `--help`, the config schema and every doc (`review.py:35-39`), and is intended for integration tests that have no TTY. But an environment variable is not a test-only mechanism: anything that can set it on a real run gets silent, unreviewed, permanent decisions.
17	
18	**Ruling needed:** leave as is and document it as an accepted cost; make the automation path report `was_interactive=False` so nothing permanent is written; or gate it on a test-only signal. Note the second option would change what the integration tests can assert.
19	
20	## DIV-03 — Passwordless-sudo preconditions differ per manager and are stated in no requirement
21	
22	The four jobs have materially different prerequisites, all enforced in `validate()` and none written down outside the code:
23	
24	| | source | target |
25	| - | - | - |
26	| apt | required | required |
27	| snap | required | required |
28	| flatpak | none | only when a system-scope item exists on either machine |
29	| manual | none | none |
30	
31	`apt_sync.py:3876-3891` records why source-side sudo is a hard failure rather than a degradation: without it the `/etc/apt` capture silently returns empty digests and the sync reports success having replicated no repository configuration. `snap_sync.py:701-706` records that the source needs it because the refresh pause writes there, and `snap_sync.py:743-745` that snapd admin-gates even *reading* snap config.
32	
33	This is a user-visible precondition — it decides whether the job can run at all — so it belongs in the requirements. **No conflict, just an omission.** The narrative states it; the articles need an entry.
34	
35	## DIV-04 — Sideloaded snaps: resolved by ruling them out of scope
36	
37	Resolved 2026-07-29. `PKG-NG-SIDELOAD` claimed sideloaded snaps "cannot be reproduced" as an accepted cost, which #221 contradicts — a snippet running `snap install --dangerous` reproduces one. The article is deleted: it described deferred work as a deliberate non-goal.
38	
39	The replacement ruling is that sideloaded snaps are out of scope entirely and ignored on both machines, rather than half-handled. `PKG-FR-SNAP-SIDELOAD` now says so, and the code's remaining half — a sideloaded snap only the target has is still an ordinary removal candidate, so the tool can offer to delete a snap it cannot reinstall — is recorded in the criteria's gap register.
40	
41	## DIV-05 — Cross-manager review is asserted in one comment and denied everywhere else
42	
43	`orchestrator.py:1293-1295` justifies the `PackageItemFailures` arm with "The user approved changes across several package managers in ONE batched review (D-24)". There is no such review. `sync_core.py:8-10` and `review.py:713-715` both state the opposite — batching is per manager, each job reviews its own groups inside its own `execute()`, and there is no coordinator.
44	
45	The behaviour the comment guards is still right (one manager's failures should not cancel another's approved work); only the stated reason is wrong. Code comment fix, no behaviour change.
46	
47	## DIV-06 — The generated decision-file header contains a leaked identifier
48	
49	`state.py:93` writes, into every user's `~/.config/pc-switcher/<manager>.decisions.yaml`:
50	
51	> This file is machine-local and is never synced to any peerfilter_inert. Remove…
52	
53	`peerfilter_inert` is a function name that ran into the sentence. Cosmetic, but it ships to users' machines in a file the requirements describe as the record of their explicit decisions.
54	
55	## DIV-07 — apt and flatpak apply the conflict screen to different candidate sets
56	
57	`PKG-FR-REPO-CONFLICT` and `PKG-FR-FLATPAK-REPOINT` read as one rule in two ecosystems. They are not quite the same rule.
58	
59	apt raises the conflict screen for **every** differing repository file that feeds a machine-specific target package, and approving it forces the write (`apt_sync.py:2267-2285`).
60	
61	flatpak additionally gates on the remote being in the set `_derive_remotes` would provision if the review approved everything — so a remote no approved ref needs is never a question, and answering "overwrite" cannot by itself make a remote travel (`flatpak_sync.py:1420-1429`). The code names this as a deliberate divergence from apt.
62	
63	The reasoning is sound — flatpak has no always-sync bucket to make a remote travel independently — but the articles state the two as symmetric. **Ruling needed:** is the asymmetry intended, and should the articles say so?
64	
65	## DIV-08 — `manual_installs_sync` is not covered by the job-ordering check
66	
67	`PKG-FR-JOB-ORDER` says "the three package-manager jobs" must precede `folder_sync`, and `orchestrator.py:1073` validates exactly those three. Code and article agree.
68	
69	The question is whether the article is right. `manual_installs_sync` also installs software — by replaying a snippet — and that software writes its own stock defaults exactly as an apt package does, which is the whole reason for the ordering rule. The shipped config lists it before `folder_sync` (`default-config.yaml:55`), so the default is correct; nothing catches a user who reorders it.
70	
71	**Ruling needed:** extend the rule to all four, or state explicitly why snippet-installed software does not need it.
72	
73	## DIV-09 — The UAT runbook describes two behaviours that have since been fixed
74	
75	`02-UAT-01-RUNBOOK.md` §4b tells the tester that choosing "Skip" at a collateral prompt "writes `SKIP_ONCE` over EVERY package in the batched removal candidate set, not only the one that produced the collateral … so it also cancels a never-offer-again tick made on `X` in the same review", and instructs them to work around it by splitting the check across two runs.
76	
77	That is no longer true. Attribution narrows the batch by re-rehearsing each candidate alone (`apt_sync.py:2528-2576`), and a skip overrides only `APPLY` decisions, explicitly leaving `SKIP_ALWAYS` intact (`apt_sync.py:2645-2666`). Fixed in `402f7067`.
78	
79	§4d likewise tells the tester to expect the title `Delete repositorys the source no longer has (apt)` and to record the pluralisation as a known cosmetic defect. That was fixed in `ffa06900`; the title now reads `Delete repositories …` (`apt_sync.py:338-341`, `apt_sync.py:2055`).
80	
81	§4a is now stale in a third way: it tells the tester that "leaving one unticked at the review is what makes the never-offer-again screen appear". That screen no longer exists — `9ba0d437` replaced the two-pass checkbox flow with one decision screen per group, where every row carries its own answer and there is no leftover set to re-offer. UAT test 1 in `02-UAT.md` describes the same superseded flow ("questionary checkbox composes with paused Rich Live, installs/removals grouped separately, removals start unticked").
82	
83	A tester following the runbook as written would report three fixes as regressions and would look for a screen that has been deliberately removed. The runbook and `02-UAT.md` both need updating before UAT runs.
84	
85	## DIV-10 — A held package is installed at the wrong version, then frozen there
86	
87	Ruled on 2026-07-29, after the code was written, so this is a known gap rather than a contradiction.
88	
89	An apt hold blocks install, upgrade and removal alike — measured on `ubuntu:24.04`: `apt-get remove` and `apt-get install` on a held package both refuse with `E: Held packages were changed`, and `autoremove` leaves it alone. It therefore carries the intent "do not move this off the version that works" as well as "do not lose this", and apt offers no way to distinguish them.
90	
91	`apt_sync` installs every package by name (`_install_args` → `apt-get install --assume-yes --no-install-recommends <name>`) and applies the hold as a separate item afterwards. So where the source holds a package the target lacks, the target installs whatever version its repositories currently offer and then freezes on it — permanently, since nothing will move a held package again. The two machines end up held at different versions with nothing reporting it.
92	
93	`PKG-FR-APT-HOLD-VERSION` now requires the source's exact version for that case, with failure naming both versions where the target cannot supply it. Recorded in the criteria's gap register.
94	
95	**Still unruled:** the same package held on *both* machines at different versions. `PKG-FR-APT-HELD-TARGET` suppresses any package-level item for a held target package, and a hold present on both sides produces no hold item either, so that divergence is currently invisible in every run. Converging it would mean unhold → install the source's version → re-hold, which is a larger change than the install case.
96	
97	## Ambiguity flagged for the Stage 5 article audit — done 2026-07-30
98	
99	`PKG-FR-MACHINE-SPECIFIC` says the item is "never to be offered again on that machine. The mark MUST be local to that machine" with no antecedent for either "that machine". The rule the code implements is the holder rule (`sync_core.py:213-223`): install and change diffs record on the source, removal diffs on the target, written through that machine's own executor. The article was unstatable without a name for the holding machine, which the narrative's vocabulary section now introduces; the article uses the term and drops its inline gloss.
100	
101	The full audit ran over all 123 articles on 2026-07-30. Ten findings, all in the criteria and all vocabulary rather than substance: `rehearsal` for the narrative's *dry run*; `provenance` for *origin*, which the criteria itself contradicted by saying *origin divergence* elsewhere; `prompts` and `a screen` for what the user is asked; `Skip-once` for the narrative's decision words; `blocks` as a collective noun the narrative never defines; `in either direction` on the banned list; two articles carrying two Why lines that said the same thing twice; and `PKG-FR-ASK-WHEN-NOT-DERIVABLE` claiming to enumerate every non-derivable question while omitting four of them. No article was found that could not be stated in the narrative's vocabulary once reworded.
102	
103	## DIV-11 — A filtered remote is replicated unfiltered
104	
105	Ruled on 2026-07-29, after the code was written, so this is a known gap rather than a contradiction.
106	
107	**Measured** (flatpak 1.14.6, `02-SPEC-snap-flatpak-derivation.md` §2.8): `flatpak remote-modify --filter=/tmp/f.filter <remote>` records the *path* `/tmp/f.filter` in the remote's `filter` column and adds a `filtered` token to `options`. The filter's content is an ordinary file at that arbitrary local path, outside the ostree store.
108	
109	The original reading was that this makes the filter unsyncable — "not repository-or-key material". It does not. The content is a file, and the run already carries files byte-for-byte: a repository's signing key is copied exactly this way. What the earlier decision actually gave up on was the *path*: it is arbitrary, so replicating the filter means the flatpak job writing to a location it does not own, possibly inside `folder_sync`'s territory.
110	
111	`PKG-FR-FLATPAK-FILTER` now requires the filter to be replicated: copied byte-for-byte to the same absolute path on the target, re-applied to the replicated remote, derived rather than reviewed, and applied after the approved applications from that remote have landed. Failure to copy or re-apply fails every approved application from that remote.
112	
113	`flatpak_sync` implements the opposite: `_FLATPAK_REMOTES_CMD_TEMPLATE` requests `name,url,options`, so the path is never read, and the shipped behaviour is one WARNING per filtered remote naming the `remote-modify --filter` command. Implementing the requirement widens the capture to four columns, which reshapes every remote fixture in the suite — with the `filter` column requested, an unfiltered remote prints four fields, not three.
114	
115	`docs/jobs/package-sync.md:252` documents the shipped warning behaviour and stays accurate until the code changes.
116	
117	**Open within this ruling:** the ordering rule is stated as a design requirement, not from measurement. Whether flatpak actually refuses to install a ref its own filter excludes has not been tested.
118	
119	## DIV-12 — A skipped removal loses its collateral protection
120	
121	Found on 2026-07-30 while checking the narrative's collateral claim against the code. This is a shipped bug, not a requirement that moved.
122	
123	`_collect_plan_time_collateral` builds `reviewed_names` from the install and removal candidate lists (`apt_sync.py:2586-2588`), before the review runs and therefore before any answer exists. `_classify_collateral` then skips every package in that set (`apt_sync.py:2670`). The comment justifies it as "a decision the user is taking anyway" — true for a removal the user approved, false for one they skipped.
124	
125	So: a package offered for removal, kept by answering *skip*, is excluded from collateral protection for the rest of the run. Approving an unrelated install whose transaction removes it deletes it with no question and, per `PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-AUTO`'s classification, no review line either. The user asked to keep it and it goes.
126	
127	`PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-MANUAL` now states that only an APPROVED removal exempts a package. Recorded in the criteria's gap register.
128	
129	## Rulings that close earlier divergences
130	
131	- **DIV-07** (apt's repository-conflict question is wider than flatpak's) is ruled: both ask only what the approved changes need. `PKG-FR-REPO-CONFLICT` now gates on the repository being one this run writes for an approved package. The code still asks more widely.
132	- **DIV-08** (`manual_installs_sync` outside the job-ordering check) is ruled: the rule covers all four package jobs. `orchestrator.py:1082` validates three.
133	- The ESM cost question behind `PKG-FR-ESM-GATE` is answered by measurement rather than ruling: on an attached Ubuntu 24.04 desktop, 60 of 2297 installed packages resolve their candidate to `esm.ubuntu.com`, including `ffmpeg`, `gimp` and `imagemagick`. The container's zero was an artefact of its package set.
134	
135	## DIV-13 — A repository credential reaches the log
136	
137	Ruled on 2026-07-30, after the code was written.
138	
139	A private PPA or a commercial repository carries its credential in the URL itself (`REDACTED`), so the URL is the secret. `Executor._announce` traces every command verbatim at DEBUG (`executor.py:154`), the repository-conflict question shows both machines' copies of a source file in full, and `PKG-FR-LOG-VERBATIM` now adds the manager's own output. Nothing in the codebase redacts anything — `grep -rn redact src/` finds no match.
140	
141	Logs are written to `~/.local/share/pc-switcher/logs` with mode `rw-rw-r--`, so the exposure is to every account on the machine that wrote the log. It does not spread: pc-switcher's own runtime files are excluded from `folder_sync` ahead of any user filter and cannot be re-included (`default-config.yaml:135-137`).
142	
143	`PKG-FR-CREDENTIAL-PRIVACY` now requires the embedded credential to be withheld wherever a URL is written or shown. Recorded in the criteria's gap register.
144	
145	Related, and already satisfied: `PKG-FR-ESM-PRIVACY` is honoured by construction rather than by filtering — `pro status --format json` is parsed and only the `attached` boolean escapes (`apt_sync.py:113-114`, `278-281`).
146	
147	## DIV-14 — The log records counts, not decisions, and no manager output at all
148	
149	Verified on 2026-07-30 against the current head, after the logging requirements were ruled on.
150	
151	`PKG-FR-LOG-DECISIONS` asks for every item a job presented together with the decision it received. What the code writes is:
152	
153	- one FULL line per item that was actually applied — `f"{diff.action.value} {diff.label}"` (`sync_core.py:493`) — or, in a dry run, one `Would …` line per item (`sync_core.py:397`);
154	- INFO counts around them: how many changes are being applied, how many succeeded, how many failed with a joined summary (`sync_core.py:385-416`);
155	- in a non-interactive run, a WARNING carrying the COUNT of unresolved items (`review.py:822`) and one line per group that was not asked (`review.py:914`).
156	
157	So an item the user skipped produces no line at all, and no line anywhere pairs an item with its decision. Auto-collateral is likewise absent — `_classify_collateral` deliberately produces "nothing, not even a report line the user cannot act on" (`apt_sync.py:2655-2656`), which `PKG-FR-COLLATERAL-AUTO` now overrides.
158	
159	`PKG-FR-LOG-VERBATIM` asks for the manager's own output verbatim in the debug log. `Executor._announce` traces the command TEXT at DEBUG before running it (`executor.py:154`); nothing traces what came back. The only output that reaches the log is `stderr` attached as structured context on error paths (`sync_core.py:489`, `apt_sync.py:3551-3557`). No stdout, at any level.
160	
161	Both are recorded in the criteria's gap register. Note the interaction with `PKG-FR-CREDENTIAL-PRIVACY` (DIV-13): implementing verbatim output without the redaction point puts repository credentials in a world-readable file, so the two land together or not at all.
162	
163	Log volume is a known consequence, not an objection: runs on the maintainer's desktop already produce 350-378 MB logs, and the ruling was "all of it, as written".
164

docs/adr/adr-020-declarative-package-convergence.md:81:The default is a three-way decision: apply / skip once / skip always — the names of the three decisions, not the words a screen shows for them (D-24 rules the wording). "Apply" is direction-dependent — missing on target means install/add/enable, extra on target means remove/delete/disable, different on both means change the target to match the source. The review names the concrete action per item (e.g. "remove brscan3", not "apply").
docs/adr/adr-020-declarative-package-convergence.md:116:### Batched review inside each job (D-24)
docs/adr/adr-020-declarative-package-convergence.md:122:As the four jobs stand, none needs a second review, which is a property of their diffs rather than a rule they obey: a package's classification depends on the SOURCE's origins, which no run mutates, so no fact a review is answered on can be invalidated by what that run writes; the one fact that does depend on this run's writes — whether the target really ends up with the source's origin — is checked by D-35 and reported as a per-item failure rather than re-asked. `apt_sync` therefore has no second review pass and needs none — nothing this section permits is an argument for adding one back. Where the facts genuinely do change, a second question is the correct answer.
docs/planning/package-sync-conformance-criteria.md:66:- **PKG-FR-BATCHED**: A job's questions SHOULD be gathered into as few reviews as the decisions allow, and where the same kind of decision recurs the items MUST be presented together and be settleable in a single pass rather than as a sequence of one-item questions.
docs/planning/package-sync-conformance-criteria.md:120:- **PKG-FR-APT-ORIGIN-DERIVED**: Approving a package MUST carry the repository, key and pins its origin needs, without a separate question and without a further question once they land.
docs/planning/package-sync-conformance-criteria.md:249:- **PKG-FR-FLATPAK-FILTER**: A remote the source restricts with a filter MUST be replicated with that filter. The filter file MUST be copied byte-for-byte from the source to the same absolute path on the target and re-applied to the replicated remote. It is derived like a signing key and MUST NOT be a review item. It MUST be applied after the approved applications from that remote have landed. A filter that cannot be copied or re-applied MUST fail every approved application from that remote, naming the remote and the path.

content.text: ADR-020 D-24 itself ends with *"Where the facts genuinely do change, a second question is the correct answer"* — it permits the loop and merely asserts today's jobs don't need one. And `PKG-FR-BATCHED` is a SHOULD. So nothing has to be overturned; the pipeline just has to grow the seam. Let me see what the reviewer protocol can already do.

# Step 1 (revised) — make the pipeline fit the jobs, then restructure `apt_sync`

## Context

The handover's Step 1 asks for a wholesale restructure of `apt_sync.py` (4053 lines, 69 methods, 35 attributes) into a prescribed module list, behaviour unchanged. Executing that literally partitions the god object without removing what makes it one: `PackageSyncJob`'s fixed `plan → review → apply` line, which apt and flatpak both work around.

The requirements narrative — the authority — already states the flow as a loop, not a line:

- `package-sync-user-requirements.md:56`: "That is a preference, not a rule: applying an approved change can reveal something the plan could not know, and a further question is then correct."
- its flow diagram (`:62-69`) carries a dashed `apply → a further question → apply` edge.
- `:52`: "Consent precedes every change" — per change, not one review before all changes.
- `PKG-FR-BATCHED` is a SHOULD.

ADR-020 D-24 permits it too (`adr-020:122`: "Where the facts genuinely do change, a second question is the correct answer"); it only asserts, as a property of today's diffs, that no job needs one. That assertion is false for apt already — `apt_sync.py:66-73` documents accepting a lesser behaviour for exactly the case the narrative says must be asked about (a D-34 class-3 install's manual collateral is discovered after the derived repository lands, and the code fails the item instead of asking, against `:165`).

Evidence the base contract misfits more than one job:

| Symptom | apt | flatpak |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No stage structure, so an ordered/transactional unit is smuggled through the per-item loop | synthetic `apt:metadata-refresh` diff + `_repo_group_outcome` latch + `_record_group_failure`, with a documented `KeyError` hazard (`apt_sync.py:3307-3315`) | "the inherited …pipeline cannot express two ordered item classes" (`flatpak_sync.py:1156`) |
| `accept_review()` is sync, so derivation cannot read the machines and `plan()` over-captures | — | `_source_ref_origins`, `_source_runtime_by_ref_id` exist only "because derivation runs in the synchronous `accept_review()`" (`flatpak_sync.py:1184-1189`) |
| Apply-time facts lazily memoised on the job behind `\| None` sentinels | `_origin_refusals`, `_repo_group_outcome`, `_metadata_refreshed` | target remotes "re-read lazily at the first ref install, discarded whenever a remote write lands" (`flatpak_sync.py:1200-1202`) |

So: change the pipeline to the one the requirements describe, then restructure `apt_sync` onto it. Module size is not a design input.

## The pipeline (`packages/sync_core.py`)

New types:

- `Round` — one consent-then-change cycle: `groups` (what must be asked before this round's changes; may be empty, in which case nothing is prompted) and `stages`.
- `Stage` — `name`, `diffs`, and ownership of its own atomicity. A stage is where "applied in the order the job requires" and "all-or-nothing" become expressible instead of commented as impossible.
- `StageReport` — per-item outcomes and failures.
- `DecisionLedger` — the run's accumulated `item_id → Decision` across rounds, plus the diffs each round proposed. Replaces `_accepted_plan`/`_accepted_outcome` and implements the narrative's "a decision made earlier in this same run counts" (`:169`) directly rather than through per-job frozen snapshots.

New hooks, replacing `plan()`/`accept_review()`/`after_review()`:

- `async open_round(ledger) -> Round | None` — the next round of work, or `None` when the run is done. Read-only. A job that needs one round returns one and then `None`.
- `async derive(round, outcome) -> None` — turn this round's decisions into the work its stages will do. **Async**, which is what removes flatpak's pre-capture and lets apt compute its derived write set against whatever it needs to read.
- `async run_stage(stage, ledger) -> StageReport` — default implementation is today's per-item `converge()` loop with `ConvergeItemFailed` collection, so snap and `manual_installs_sync` implement nothing new.

`execute()` becomes the loop: open round → review its groups (non-interactive, abort and `SKIP_ALWAYS`-recording rules unchanged) → merge into the ledger → `derive` → run each stage in order → next round. Failures raise `PackageItemFailures` once, after the last round.

What each job gets: snap and manual-installs, one round with one stage (inherited). flatpak, one round with three ordered stages (remotes+refs, filters, masks) — `PKG-FR-FLATPAK-FILTER`'s ordering stops being a comment. apt, one round of three stages (`/etc/apt` unit, packages, holds) plus a second round when the run derived repositories.

## apt module layout — `src/pcswitcher/jobs/apt_sync/`

A package, not `jobs/apt/`: `Orchestrator._resolve_sync_job_class` (`orchestrator.py:706`) does `import_module(f"pcswitcher.jobs.{job_name}")` and scans `dir(module)` for `name == "apt_sync"`, so the importable name must stay `apt_sync` and `__init__.py` re-exports `AptSyncJob` plus today's `__all__` (`AptTransactionPreview`, `simulate_apt_transaction`). `__init__.py` also holds the package narrative from the current module docstring.

Cut by phase, not by subsystem: reads produce frozen snapshots, planning is a pure function of them, deriving is a pure function of (plan, decisions), and only the stages touch a machine.

| --- | --- |
| `job.py` | `AptSyncJob`: `open_round`, `derive`, `run_stage`, review-group carving, `validate` |
| `paths.py` | the `/etc/apt` locations, distro/ESM filename sets, key directories, item_id ↔ path |

- `:52`: "Consent precedes every change" — per change, not one review before all changes.

| Symptom | apt | flatpak |

## The pipeline (`packages/sync_core.py`)

New types:

- `Round` — one consent-then-change cycle: `groups` (what must be asked before this round's changes; may be empty, in which case nothing is prompted) and `stages`.

Right to ask. Auditing it honestly, three of the four new abstractions don't earn their keep:

- **`Round` + `open_round`** — over-engineered. The capability needed is "ask more questions mid-apply". `review_items` already handles the non-interactive path and abort internally, so an extra question inherits those rules for free. The only thing that isn't free is recording a `SKIP_ALWAYS` answered late. That's one base method, `ask_more(groups) -> decisions`, ~20 lines — not a control-flow rewrite.
- **`DecisionLedger`** — over-engineered. `_accepted_outcome.decisions` is already the run's decision map; a late answer merges into it.
- **`Stage` / `StageReport`** — over-engineered. What apt and flatpak actually lack is permission to own their apply order. Decomposing `apply()` (pull the per-item loop out as `_converge_batch(diffs)`, move the single raise to the end) gives that with no new types, and the marker diff and latch die anyway because apt's `apply()` then drives the order directly.

Also 16 modules was two too many: `paths.py` folds into `items.py` (an item's identity and where its file lives are one fact) and `snapshot.py` into `probe.py` (frozen facts and the reads producing them always change together).

The one thing I'd defend at full size is the phase cut — reads → frozen facts → pure planning — but I'll flag that its testability payoff is a hypothesis I haven't measured, and it's reachable incrementally by passing facts in rather than reading them off `self`.

Net: same capability and the same deletions, roughly a third of the new machinery.

## Context

The handover's Step 1 asks for a wholesale restructure of `apt_sync.py` (4053 lines, 69 methods, 35 attributes), behaviour unchanged. Executing that literally partitions the god object without removing what makes it one: `PackageSyncJob` fixes the order and shape of apply, and apt and flatpak both work around it.

The requirements narrative — the authority — states the flow as a loop, not a line:

- `package-sync-user-requirements.md:56`: "That is a preference, not a rule: applying an approved change can reveal something the plan could not know, and a further question is then correct."
- its flow diagram (`:62-69`) carries a dashed `apply → a further question → apply` edge.
- `:52`: "Consent precedes every change" — per change, not one review before all changes.
- `PKG-FR-BATCHED` is a SHOULD.

ADR-020 D-24 permits it (`adr-020:122`: "Where the facts genuinely do change, a second question is the correct answer"); it only asserts, as a property of today's diffs, that no job needs one. That assertion is already false for apt: `apt_sync.py:66-73` documents accepting a lesser behaviour for exactly the case the narrative says must be asked about — a D-34 class-3 install's manual collateral is discoverable only after the derived repository lands, and the code fails the item instead of asking (against `:165`).

Evidence the base contract misfits more than one job:

| Symptom | apt | flatpak |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No way to own apply order, so an ordered/transactional unit is smuggled through the per-item loop | synthetic `apt:metadata-refresh` diff + `_repo_group_outcome` latch + `_record_group_failure`, with a documented `KeyError` hazard (`apt_sync.py:3307-3315`) | "the inherited …pipeline cannot express two ordered item classes" (`flatpak_sync.py:1156`) |
| `accept_review()` is sync, so derivation cannot read the machines and `plan()` over-captures | — | `_source_ref_origins`, `_source_runtime_by_ref_id` exist only "because derivation runs in the synchronous `accept_review()`" (`flatpak_sync.py:1184-1189`) |
| Apply-time facts lazily memoised on the job behind `\| None` sentinels | `_origin_refusals`, `_repo_group_outcome`, `_metadata_refreshed` | target remotes "re-read lazily at the first ref install, discarded whenever a remote write lands" (`flatpak_sync.py:1200-1202`) |

Module size is not a design input.

## The pipeline change (`packages/sync_core.py`) — two methods, no new types

This is the whole of the narrative's loop.
- `apply()` decomposed: the per-item iteration becomes `async _converge_batch(diffs) -> list[failure]`, and the single `PackageItemFailures` raise moves to the end of `apply()`. A job that needs its own order overrides `apply()` and calls the pieces.

Nothing else changes: `plan()`, `accept_review()`, `converge()`, `after_review()`, the dry-run contract, the D-26 rules and `execute()` all keep their present shape. snap and `manual_installs_sync` are untouched.

## Approved Plan:
# Step 1 (revised) — let the jobs own their apply order, then restructure `apt_sync`

## Context

The handover's Step 1 asks for a wholesale restructure of `apt_sync.py` (4053 lines, 69 methods, 35 attributes), behaviour unchanged. Executing that literally partitions the god object without removing what makes it one: `PackageSyncJob` fixes the order and shape of apply, and apt and flatpak both work around it.

The requirements narrative — the authority — states the flow as a loop, not a line:

- `package-sync-user-requirements.md:56`: "That is a preference, not a rule: applying an approved change can reveal something the plan could not know, and a further question is then correct."
- its flow diagram (`:62-69`) carries a dashed `apply → a further question → apply` edge.
- `:52`: "Consent precedes every change" — per change, not one review before all changes.
- `PKG-FR-BATCHED` is a SHOULD.

ADR-020 D-24 permits it (`adr-020:122`: "Where the facts genuinely do change, a second question is the correct answer"); it only asserts, as a property of today's diffs, that no job needs one. That assertion is already false for apt: `apt_sync.py:66-73` documents accepting a lesser behaviour for exactly the case the narrative says must be asked about — a D-34 class-3 install's manual collateral is discoverable only after the derived repository lands, and the code fails the item instead of asking (against `:165`).

Evidence the base contract misfits more than one job:

| Symptom | apt | flatpak |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No way to own apply order, so an ordered/transactional unit is smuggled through the per-item loop | synthetic `apt:metadata-refresh` diff + `_repo_group_outcome` latch + `_record_group_failure`, with a documented `KeyError` hazard (`apt_sync.py:3307-3315`) | "the inherited …pipeline cannot express two ordered item classes" (`flatpak_sync.py:1156`) |
| `accept_review()` is sync, so derivation cannot read the machines and `plan()` over-captures | — | `_source_ref_origins`, `_source_runtime_by_ref_id` exist only "because derivation runs in the synchronous `accept_review()`" (`flatpak_sync.py:1184-1189`) |
| Apply-time facts lazily memoised on the job behind `\| None` sentinels | `_origin_refusals`, `_repo_group_outcome`, `_metadata_refreshed` | target remotes "re-read lazily at the first ref install, discarded whenever a remote write lands" (`flatpak_sync.py:1200-1202`) |

Module size is not a design input.

## The pipeline change (`packages/sync_core.py`) — two methods, no new types

- `async ask_more(groups) -> Mapping[str, Decision]`: review extra groups mid-apply, record any `SKIP_ALWAYS` through the existing `_record_permanent_skips` path, merge into `self._accepted_outcome.decisions`, return them. `review_items` already owns the non-interactive path (every item `SKIP_ONCE`, `was_interactive=False`) and the abort semantics, so an extra question inherits both. This is the whole of the narrative's loop.
- `apply()` decomposed: the per-item iteration becomes `async _converge_batch(diffs) -> list[failure]`, and the single `PackageItemFailures` raise moves to the end of `apply()`. A job that needs its own order overrides `apply()` and calls the pieces.

Nothing else changes: `plan()`, `accept_review()`, `converge()`, `after_review()`, the dry-run contract, the D-26 rules and `execute()` all keep their present shape. snap and `manual_installs_sync` are untouched.

Separately and on its own merit: make `accept_review()` async, which removes flatpak's documented pre-capture (`:1184-1189`). Not needed by apt; its own commit.

## apt module layout — `src/pcswitcher/jobs/apt_sync/`

A package, not `jobs/apt/`: `Orchestrator._resolve_sync_job_class` (`orchestrator.py:706`) does `import_module(f"pcswitcher.jobs.{job_name}")` and scans `dir(module)` for `name == "apt_sync"`, so the importable name must stay `apt_sync` and `__init__.py` re-exports `AptSyncJob` plus today's `__all__` (`AptTransactionPreview`, `simulate_apt_transaction`). `__init__.py` also holds the package narrative from the current module docstring.

Cut by phase: reads produce frozen facts, planning and deriving are pure over them, and only the last four modules touch a machine.

| Module | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `job.py` | `AptSyncJob`: `plan`, `accept_review`, `apply` (owns the order), `converge`, review-group carving, `validate` |
| `items.py` | the five item dataclasses, id prefixes, id parsing, the `/etc/apt` locations and id ↔ path |
| `messages.py` | the nine `build_*` |
| `commands.py` | apt-get/apt-cache/apt-mark/dpkg command construction, `--dry-run` parsing |
| `probe.py` | every batched read, and the frozen fact objects it returns |
| `origins.py` | D-34 classification, D-35 verification |
| `diffing.py` | every diff builder |
| `collateral.py` | D-30 rehearsal, classification, attribution, apply-time guards |
| `derived.py` | which `/etc/apt` files travel and why (D-37/38/39) + package attribution |
| `keyrings.py` | D-12 |
| `etc_apt.py` | the transactional unit: backup → write → refresh → rollback |
| `packages.py` | install/remove/hold convergence, the guard chain |
| `files.py` | every target file mutation: stage→promote, backup, remove |
| `esm_gate.py` | the D-38 gate |

## Member map

`Deleted` means the member stops existing, not that it moves; the commit that removes it is named. Collaborators receive captured facts as frozen objects rather than reading them off the job — that is what makes the planning half testable without an executor fake (expectation, not measured).

Preserve the hedge and the exception clause when rewriting; if a clause looks like clutter, that is usually the nuance. Before I start writing, one reordering I should flag rather than do silently.

C2 as written keeps the marker diff *and* has `apply()` drive the order — those are redundant together, and the base hooks (`ask_more`, `_converge_batch`) would have no consumer until C4/C5, both of which land after the Step-2 sweep. Building a seam before its consumer is the same mistake I just cut twice. So:

- **C1 becomes the apt restructure itself** — pure relocation, `apply()` unchanged, marker and latch intact. That is what Step 1 asks for and what unblocks the sweep.
- `ask_more`, `_converge_batch` and async `accept_review` land in C4/C5 **with their first consumer**, where the behaviour they enable justifies and tests them.

The architecture and the deletion list are unchanged; only the build order is.
